# ADHD

A conversation in small turns, for a reader who loses the thread in long messages. It works for anyone who wants it short. You answer in a few lines, ask one question and wait. Stay in this shape until the owner says stop or calls another skill.

Done when the owner has what they came for: an answer, a decision, or a brief they said go to. Then one line says what was settled and what comes next.

## The shape of a turn

- At most three points, one idea per line. No headings, no preamble, and nothing that repeats what they just said.
- End with one question at most, with your best guess as the answer, so "yes" or one word is enough. With real options, number two or three and mark the one you would pick.
- Wait for the answer before the next question. Never ask two.
- A question is for what you cannot decide. A reversible choice you make and say in one line: "Going with A. Say if not."
- More than six lines of material: give the first three and end with "Say `more` for the rest."
- A tangent, theirs or yours: park it in one line, "Parked: <it>", and go on. Read the parked lines back at a pause, or when asked.
- A reply that is not an answer ("hm", "what?", "idk"): say the same question again in fewer words, with the guess attached. Do not add another.
- "Shorter" halves the next turn.

## Steps

1. Start in the first reply, with no greeting. A question in the message: answer it in the shape above. An idea: step 3. Nothing: with a run in this folder, ask whether to pick it up, and without one ask "What are we working on?". A run is here when `100x status` works and shows a Stage past `0 Open` or at least one decision. A bare `100x init` shows neither.
2. A question about a project or a run: read first. `100x status`, `.100x/STATE.md`, the last five rows of `.100x/decisions.tsv`, `git log --oneline -5` and the files the question names. Answer from what you read, never from memory, and say in one line what you could not find. Use the owner's plain words, the phrases in `100x ref words`: `100x status` prints internal names, so never paste its lines. Where a run stands comes out as three points: where it is, what is next, and what waits on the owner.
3. An idea: shape it into a brief, one question at a time. The moment, the signature moment that makes someone want it. Who it is for. The one thing that must not break. What to leave out. Skip any the idea already answers. After each answer say the brief so far in two lines at most. Ask four questions at the most, then say "Assuming <x>" for what is left.
4. Go. The owner says go, or "build it": follow the `100x` skill from Stage 0 with the brief you shaped together, or the mode skill they name. Nothing builds before that word, and a question about the idea is not a go. The shape stays on while you build, so the final message is short too.
5. With a run in this folder, write each decision the owner makes: `100x log frame "<what they chose>" "<why, in their words>" "the owner said so in this thread"`. When the talk ends, write the parked lines in one row: `100x log frame "parked: <them>" "tangents, not decided"`. With no run, create nothing.
6. Stop when the owner says stop, calls another skill, or has an answer and nothing is open. One line: what was settled, and what comes next.

The `100x-status` skill gives the same answer in one shot, in its six line shape and with no back and forth.

# Bake-off

Does the same agent make prototypes that a blind judge prefers when it follows the 100x-mockup skill, compared with the same agent without it? This skill runs that test and reports what came out, including when nothing could be shown. It builds no prototype of its own and never argues for the skill. Today it runs only through the Cursor SDK, because every arm and judge starts with `100x helper run`. Where that is not set up, step 1 says what to run, and nothing runs on a stand-in.

Two arms, `skill-off` and `skill-on`, make the same briefs under the same model and the same 20 minutes. Each pair is judged twice with A and B swapped, from folders that carry no arm name. The key that says which arm is which is sealed with a hash first, and the hash is signed with this machine's 100x key. The word is "ahead" only with at least 6 decisive pairs, an exact sign test under 0.05, and a judge that passed two controls. Otherwise it is "not shown", with the reason. The tool decides the word and you never do.

Done when `100x eval bakeoff score` has written `report.md`, the report sits in `docs/evals/` with a picture of each pair, and the reply carries the counts and the verdict line of `score` word for word, and every caution under it. A report that says "not shown" is a finished bake-off.

## Steps

1. The helper. `100x helper models` is the check: it lists the model ids, or says why it cannot. `The Cursor SDK is not installed. Run `100x helper setup` once.` means run `100x helper setup`. `The Cursor SDK has no valid login.` means run `100x helper login` once, which opens a browser to approve this machine, or set `CURSOR_API_KEY`. Run the one it names and `100x helper models` again, and do not go on until it lists models. When it still cannot, stop with the line it printed and the one step that is the owner's, which is the login. The pairs step photographs every page, so `100x eval bakeoff init` prints a Browsers line when no Chromium is installed. Run `100x browsers` before any arm starts, not after.
2. Read `evals/PROTOCOL.md` in the 100x repo. `100x eval bakeoff init` prints its path. It fixes the rule for the word and names the threats. Once an arm has started, change nothing in it. A change is an amendment at the bottom.
3. One model. The protocol wants the same model for every arm and judge, the one the owner's rules name, or the model this thread runs on when no rule names one, and the first line of the reply says which. Every arm and judge starts through the Cursor SDK with `100x helper run`, never with the Task tool and never with `cursor-agent`. `100x ref apps` says why. Use the id exactly as `100x helper models` lists it, with the effort and context the rule gives. A rule that names `muse-wonder-1.0-max`, for example, is `--model muse-wonder-1.0 --effort max --context 300k`. The window is always named and never 1m, because a 1m window or no window is MAX mode and `100x helper run` refuses it. Start one small helper first, `100x helper run --model <id> --effort <level> --context <size> --task "Reply with the word ok."`. Exit code 3 means the SDK reports another model. Stop, say so in one line, and give the owner the one decision. When the result reports no model, no receipt can be made from it, and the word is withheld for that run. Say so.
4. Folder. Somewhere neutral, never under `.100x` and never with `100x` in the path, because a judge sees its path. `100x eval bakeoff init <dir> --first 3 --pin` is the pilot, and no `--first` runs all twenty briefs, which is the run that can say "ahead". `init` prints what that costs in tokens and time and how many decisive pairs to expect, so say it to the owner before the first arm starts. `--pin` freezes the skill and tells the second arm to use it. `100x log` the seed, the folder and the pinned commit.
5. The arms, one helper at a time, in the order init printed. For each run:
   - `100x eval bakeoff mark <dir> <brief>/<arm> start`. Then start a fresh helper with `100x helper run --model <id> --effort <level> --context <size> --task-file <dir>/tasks/<brief>--<arm>.md --cwd <that run's folder, as `100x eval bakeoff status <dir>` prints it> --minutes 20 --receipt <dir>/helper-receipts/<brief>--<arm>.json --json`, with `block_until_ms` 0 in Cursor, and wait for its finished notice. It gets the text of that task file and nothing else, and it must not see the other arm, the protocol or this skill.
   - When it ends, `--minutes` has already stopped it at its deadline. Exit code 3 voids the run, and `modelCheck` says why. Then `100x eval bakeoff mark <dir> <brief>/<arm> stop --receipt <dir>/helper-receipts/<brief>--<arm>.json`. The receipt is the SDK's result in a file this machine's 100x key signed, and `mark` takes the model asked for, the model and settings that ran and the tokens from it. Never type them with `--ran`: a name typed by hand is counted as the helper's word, and the word "ahead" is not printed over it. The minutes come from the clock and never from what a helper says.
   - A run that ends with no `index.html` failed. Do not open the folder, do not write the page and do not start the run again. Go on to the next run.
6. `100x eval bakeoff pairs <dir>`. It builds the pairs and both controls, scans every judge folder for the skill's name and the arm names, seals the key and prints its hash. Log the hash now, before any judge starts. The scan reads what each file holds, whatever its name ends in, and searches a binary file for every name, except that a compressed picture is not searched for the four-letter `100x`. It reads `skill_on` and `skill- on` as the name, and `unreviewed` and `mockup` too, because a run may write them on its own page and a judge that reads them can tell the arms apart (five of the twenty pages in the 2026-11-21 run did, though the skill only asks for the label on the card and in the final message). Each task tells both arms to leave them off the page. A brief that is itself about a mockup lets `mockup` through with `--allow`. It refuses a symbolic link and a file over 25 MB, because it cannot check them. A page's title, its attributes and a picture that shows a name are not in the text it showed, so they pass. `--no-capture` runs no page at all, so a name a script builds in the browser passes too: use it for tests, and never for a run whose result will be quoted. When it refuses it names a file and a line. Remove only the words it names from that arm's folder, log each edit with its file and line, and run `pairs` again with `--edit "<file and what you removed>"` once for each. The key's scan record keeps the edits and `score` cautions about them, so the report says a person touched the pages. Say in the reply that the folders were edited. Nothing is built and no key exists until the scan passes.

# Continue

Pick up the unfinished run in this folder. Nothing new is planned and nothing is asked. A watchdog message and a retried night child ask for the same thing. A retried night mockup is the one exception: it starts its mockup again and never calls this skill.

Done when the run is back at work from its last true state, or you told the owner in one line why there is nothing to pick up.

## Steps

1. Run `100x status`. Read `.100x/STATE.md`, `.100x/project.md` (the asks, the moment, the modifiers, and its rules and do-nots when it has them), the last ten rows of `.100x/decisions.tsv` and `git log --oneline -10`.
2. Decide by what you found.
   - No `.100x` folder, or no run in it: say so in one line and ask for the brief.
   - `100x status` says FINISHED: say so in one line with the verdict and point to `100x-report`. Start no work. When the owner added an ask, treat it as a new brief and run `100x init --fresh` first.
   - NOT FINISHED: go on.
3. Do not run `100x init` or `100x log --start`. They would begin a second run. Log one row: `100x log resume "continuing at <stage>" "<why it stopped, or that the owner said continue>" "<the Stage line of STATE.md, as written>"`.
4. Read the modifiers and the mode in `project.md`. A night run (`Mode: overnight`) or a fill clock: follow the `100x-overnight` skill, and arm the watchdog again when `.100x/watchdog.json` is missing. A mockup (`run.json` says mode mockup) keeps the `100x-mockup` skill and skips step 5, because a mockup never updates `STATE.md`, so its `Next:` line is still the one `100x init` wrote. Look at what the folder holds (`index.html`, screenshots, `MOCKUP.md`), go on at the first step of that skill the folder does not show as done, keep its 15 minute clock (`100x clock`) and start no judge. A grind (`Grind: yes`) keeps the `100x-grind` skill: when `100x config print` shows `review.grind` off, turn it on again, and go on at step 4 of that skill. A wrap up (`WRAPUP.md`, tag `100x/wrapup`) keeps the `100x-wrapup` skill. A solo run (`run.json` says mode solo) keeps the `100x-solo` skill: start no helper, go on at `Next:` in `STATE.md`, and let `100x solo check` say which challenge files are still owed.
5. Go on at `Next:` in `STATE.md`. When the code disagrees with it (uncommitted changes, a half made file), finish or undo that one step first, then make `STATE.md` true again.
6. Reply in at most three lines: where the run stood (the stage in plain words, from `100x ref words`), what you do now, the time left when a clock runs. Then keep working.

# Grind

Judge, fix, judge again, for as long as it takes. The usual review stops after `review.rounds` rounds, whatever the last judge said. A grind stops when a fresh judge says the product is ready to ship.

The green light is a ship test (the last lens, over everything) where the judge writes "Ready to ship: yes" and lists no blocker and no major finding. A judge that gave no answer has not said yes. `100x triage` decides this from the files, so nobody argues it.

Done when `100x triage` said Green light and `100x finish` accepted the run. Or the grind stopped on a stall, the round limit or the clock, the final message says which in plain words, and the run is finished that way.

## Steps

1. Read the message and `100x status`. A solo run (`run.json` says mode solo) cannot grind, because the green light has to come from a fresh judge and this model cannot be one. Say so in one line and stop.
   - A brief: this is a normal build with the grind on. Follow the `100x` skill from Stage 0. Its step 6 turns the grind on once the folder exists.
   - No brief and a run in this folder: grind it. A run still before stage 6 goes through the `100x-continue` skill first. A run that already finished is ground anyway and finished again at the end, which replaces its report and its row.
   - No brief and no run: one line asking for the brief. Create nothing.
2. For a run that exists, turn it on now. `100x config set review.grind true --local`, write `Grind: yes` under Modifiers in `.100x/project.md`, and log it with `100x log frame "grind until a judge says yes" "<why>"`. Number phrases work as in the router: `5 rounds of judging` sets the usual rounds that come before the extra ones.
3. Send the pre-flight. For a build it is the router's step 8, and its time line says there is no end time: it ends on a green light, after three ship tests in a row that bring nothing better, or at 15 rounds. For a run that exists it is at most four lines: where the run stands, how many rounds are held and what the last judge said (`100x status`), that same stop line, and one "call X to change Y" line.
4. Run the rounds. Follow the `100x-judge` skill for each one, which is `100x brief`, the judge, the answers in `triage.md`, the fixes, then `100x triage`, and never shorten a round. With the grind on, `100x triage` keeps planning another ship test after the usual rounds until one is green. Read its last line:
   - `Next, 100x brief for round N`: start the next round. After the usual rounds it begins with "Not green yet."
   - `Green light`: step 6.
   - `Stalled` or `Round limit`: step 7.
   - A run that already holds rounds gets the same words from `100x brief` when its grind is over.
5. Fix between rounds.
   - Fix every accepted finding at its cause, blockers first, and run the thing again to see it hold.
   - A finding that comes back means your fix missed the cause. Reproduce the judge's evidence before you edit, and try a different fix, never the same one again.
   - A finding you reject with evidence still counts in the numbers until the next judge drops it. Put the evidence in `triage.md` and let the judge read it.
   - Never edit `findings.md`, never ask a judge for a yes, never write your own opinion of readiness into the brief. The yes has to come from a fresh judge looking at the real product.
   - Build what a finding asks for and nothing else. A grind is not a licence to add features.
   - Keep `.100x/STATE.md` true after every round (the stage, the round, `Next:`) and send long output to files. A grind outlives a context window, and the `100x-continue` skill picks it up from that file.
6. Green. The run is marked reviewed. Do the stages that are left in the `100x` skill, ship and then `100x finish`. A run that finished before gets its facts made true again first: the fixes changed the product, so run the final screens again (`100x shots`), look at them, and update `run.json` where a number or a screenshot changed, as `100x ref finish` says. Then `100x finish` replaces its report and its row. Last, `100x config set review.grind false --local`.
7. Stalled, limit or no room on the clock. Stop and do not ask another judge. A stall is three ship tests in a row that found nothing better than the best one so far, which counts blockers and majors first and findings second. `100x review-call` says when the clock has no room, and then you run the `100x run set review` command it prints, as in the `100x-judge` skill. Finish with `100x finish`, which shows the judge's no on the report like any other run, then turn the grind off as in step 6. In the final message say what the judges keep saying, in at most three lines, what you tried, and the one decision that is the owner's.
8. No judge. A grind with no judge is a build with no judge. Follow "When the call fails" in the `100x-judge` skill, finish UNREVIEWED with the reason, and say that no judge green lit it.

## Reply

The output of `100x finish` is the final message. Put one line above it: "Green light after N rounds." or "Stopped after N rounds, <why>. <the one decision>." Point to `100x-report` for the gallery. No questions.

# Judge

Judge rounds on what is already built. Nothing new builds.

The model that built a prototype shares its own blind spots. A second model that runs the thing and reads it with fresh eyes catches what the builder explained away. It is asked one question, "is this ready to ship, be brutal", in rounds. The judge looks, you fix, a fresh judge looks again and checks your fixes. `review.rounds` sets how many, 5 by default. Round by round the lens moves from the code and how it behaves, to the UI and UX, and the last round is the ship test over everything. A clean round skips the rest of its lens. It is the only second agent a run starts by default. No setting about helpers or counts limits it, and only `review.enabled false` turns it off. Never skip it because you expect a limit. Try to start it. The `100x-grind` skill is this skill with no round count: the rounds go on until a judge says yes.

In a solo run (`run.json` says mode solo) no second model starts, so skip steps 5 and 6, the check of the model that ran, and the section "When the call fails": nothing can fail to start and nothing falls back. `100x review-call` says so, and the rounds are written challenges by this model: follow `100x ref solo` for them, the log rows of steps 4 and 10 included, worded there as a self-review. `review.model` is this chat's own model, never one a check names.

Done when `100x triage` says all rounds are done, every accepted finding is fixed and re-checked, and the run is marked reviewed, or it is UNREVIEWED with the reason.

The same judge also sits in every loop, not only here. Each polish pass and each fill round asks a fresh judge the brutal question through `100x review-call --loop <name>`, with the ask at `.100x/loops/<name>/ask.md` and the answers at `answers.md`. The polish and fill references say when. Start and wait for a loop judge exactly as in steps 5 and 6 below, with the loop's 20 minute deadline. A loop judge adapts to its loop: it judges what a user sees with its eyes on the single screenshots and never from code, runs flows end to end, and tests numbers with its own inputs. Its first line says how it judged.

Before each round run `100x clock`. `100x review-call` sizes `deadlineMinutes` to the clock, at most `review.timeoutMinutes`, so a run with an hour left still gets a short review and not none. A judge needs 15 minutes. The last fifth of a plain deadline belongs to wrap up and a fill clock keeps 5 minutes for triage and finish, so the judge never runs into them. When `review-call` says there is no room, stop the rounds, run the `100x run set review` command it prints, and finish, which then only warns.

1. `100x review-call`. If it says review is off, run the `100x run set review` command it prints, which records `unreviewed` with that reason, log it, and stop. It also prints `via`, which decides step 5, and the round and its lens. When it says the judge is the model that builds (`selfReview` in `--json`), that look is a self-review. Say so in the step 4 row and the review note, and offer the owner `100x-setup` to change it. With no judge chosen it says so and prints no `via`, and step 5's `none` bullet applies. "All rounds are done" means go to step 9 and finish.
2. Commit or save all work. The reviewer shares this checkout, so uncommitted files are visible to it. Stop your own dev server so its port is free.
3. `100x brief`. It opens the next round, archives the last one and carries the earlier findings with your answers to the judge. Skim the top of `.100x/review/brief.md`. # Mockup

The owner wants to see the idea, not read about it. A mockup is the idea as running code: something to look at and click, fast.

Only one thing has to really work: the moment. Everything else can be fake, static or hard-coded, and never has to work. Code quality does not count in this mode. Licenses still apply: use your own art, art you may reuse, or a placeholder marked as one, and name anything borrowed in `MOCKUP.md` so it gets replaced before building properly. No judge looks at it, not in loops and not at the end. The owner does, in the morning gallery. The run ends marked UNREVIEWED and says so.

Done when it runs from one command, you have looked at its screenshots, `MOCKUP.md` says whether the idea holds, it is committed, and `100x finish` has accepted the run, so it shows on the report page. Aim for 15 minutes, never past 30.

## Steps

1. Model. `100x config target quick`. When it prints a model and your app shows this thread on another model or a lower effort, say so in one plain line and carry on. Never switch or wait.
2. Folder. In an empty folder, build there. Inside an existing project, use `mockups/<slug>/`. Otherwise `./<slug>/`. `100x init` (with `--fresh` when it says an earlier run is here), then `100x clock set +15m` and `100x run set mode mockup`, so a status check, a continue and a retried night child know from the first minute that this run is a mockup. A night child keeps this clock too, not the night's deadline.
3. The question. One sentence, "Does <thing> feel <way>?". It decides what to build and what to fake. `100x log --start <slug>-<yyyymmdd-hhmm>`, then `100x log start "<question>" "<why this reading>"`. Write `.100x/project.md` short: the brief word for word, the goal in one line, the `## Asks` ledger with one `- [ ]` line per ask, and the moment. The prompt sections of stage 0 and `100x prompt check` do not apply to a mockup. Never ask the owner anything. Infer. The 100x skill's 12 line pre-flight does not apply here. Send one line instead, "Mockup: does <thing> feel <way>? Back in about 15 minutes. Call 100x for a full build.", and start building. When the brief also asked for time, versions, rounds of judging or helpers, add "Dropped: <what they asked for>." to that line, because a mockup has none of them.
4. Smallest stack. One `index.html` with inline CSS and JavaScript, no install and no build, unless the question needs a server or the project's own framework. A single file needs no server: the run command is `open index.html` and `100x shots index.html` reads the file. With a server, use the dev-server rule in the 100x skill (a background job of your shell tool, never a trailing `&`).
5. Fake the rest. Hard-coded data, stub APIs, no login, no saving. Real art for the one moment that matters, never gray boxes. Pick one named look from `100x ref looks` in ten seconds and use its palette and type. A taste fork gets a switch only when both sides take under a minute.
6. Look once. `100x shots <file or url> --label mockup --viewports 390x844@3,1440x900@1`, then open the screenshots. Then one more run with `--steps` that does the key moment (click, wait, shot) and look at that too. Fix what is blank, clipped or broken once. No second pass, no loop judge.
7. Mark it. `100x run set review '{"status":"unreviewed","note":"mockup mode, no judges by design"}'`. Nobody later mistakes this for a reviewed build, and `100x finish` does not look for a judge.
8. Write `MOCKUP.md`. The idea, the question, the verdict (`holds`, `unclear` or `does not hold`) with one line of why, the run command, three things to check, what is fake, what to replace before building properly (borrowed art and fonts, with where they came from), and a paragraph that can be pasted after the 100x skill name to build it properly.
9. Close. Stop any server and commit. Close the asks with evidence, fill `run.json` as `100x ref finish` says, and run `100x finish`. A mockup has no polish passes (`polishPasses` 0), needs no must-not-break check, and has no judge. `100x finish` turns back a mockup that has polish passes, no `MOCKUP.md`, or no short clock set in its first minutes. Add one quick check only when a wrong answer would make the idea a lie, such as money, scores or dates. The verdict is `ship` when the moment lands, `fine` when it works and the moment does not land, `dud` (shown as "Needs work") when the idea does not hold. Then `100x log done "<verdict>" "<why>" "<screenshot path>" done`.

## Reply

Six lines at most. The verdict first, then the run command, then the screenshot path, then `MOCKUP.md`. No questions.

## Rules

- No judges, no deploy, no tests beyond "it loads and the key moment works".
- Code quality does not count. Spaghetti is fine. Nothing in a mockup gets reused.
- A licence question never stops a mockup, and the licence still applies. Use your own art, anything you may reuse, or a placeholder marked as one. Anything else that makes it look right goes in `MOCKUP.md` under "Replace before building properly", with where it came from. Never keep another product's logo or art in a mockup the owner might share.
- Only the moment has to work. Dead buttons and fake screens are fine when they do not block it.
- No sound. Mute every browser you drive.
- No subagents, no versions, no `for N hours`, no rounds of judging.
- A mockup that cannot answer its question in 30 minutes is a finding. Say what blocked it in `MOCKUP.md` and stop.

# Overnight

Nobody answers until morning, so every run has to finish or end in a stated block. One brief runs in this thread. Several briefs run as one child per brief, because one thread cannot hold many full runs.

Done when every brief has a finished run or a stated block, the watchdog is deleted, and the final message is the ranking from the `100x-report` skill. With fill, no run finishes before the work time is over.

## Steps

1. Briefs. Split what the owner wrote into separate ideas. Wake time from the owner's words. With none, use 07:00 and log it. Never ask what a brief means: take the most reasonable reading and log it. With no brief at all there is nothing to read, so ask for one and start nothing until it comes. A length of work ("work for 10 hours", "use all night") means use all of it, called fill. The wake time is then that length from now.
2. Model. `100x config target overnight` is the model for the children. Empty means they follow this thread, except where `helper.only` is set: then `100x night next` hands out the locked selection, never an empty target. Calling this skill is the owner's consent for children. An app with no subagent tool runs the first brief here and lists the rest as not started.
3. One brief. Run the pipeline of the `100x` skill here, record `Mode: overnight` under Modifiers in `project.md`, and send its pre-flight (step 8, at most 12 lines). Follow `100x ref unattended` for how to decide without asking. After `100x init` run `100x clock set <wake time>`, or for fill `100x clock set "<the length>" --fill`, for example `100x clock set "for 10 hours" --fill`. Arm the watchdog, see `100x ref watchdog`. With fill, after the first working version follow `100x ref fill` until `100x finish` accepts. Finish with `100x finish`. Skip the rest of this list.
4. Several briefs.
   - `100x night start --until <wake time> --brief "<text>" ...`, or `--file` for a file with briefs separated by a line of `---`. It makes one folder per brief. A brief the owner wants as a mockup goes in with `--mockup "<text>"` and runs with `100x-mockup`. No word inside a brief decides that. `--parallel N` sets how many run at once, 2 by default. `--fill` makes every child use all the time, so set `--parallel` to the number of briefs.
   - Arm the watchdog for this thread, see `100x ref watchdog`. Children arm none.
   - Send a pre-flight of at most 8 lines, for several briefs only. How many briefs, the wake time, how many at once, the model in plain words. Keep working.
5. The loop, in your own turn, until nothing is waiting or running, or the wake time comes.
   - `100x night next --json`. When it has `delegateTask`, start it with your app's subagent tool unchanged, then `100x night record <slug> <taskId>` and log the start. In Cursor start it with `100x helper run` from `100x ref apps`, never the Task tool. When it says `none`, wait.
   - Wait the way `100x ref apps` says, then `100x night status`. Where the app wakes your thread when a child ends, do other work and end the turn. Elsewhere `sleep 240` in the shell and look again. A call that waits on a child gives up after about a minute, so do not use one.
   - A child that ended while its project is not finished is retried once. `100x night next --retry <slug>`, start it, record it. After two attempts, `100x night block <slug> "<what its log shows>"`.
   - Child output stays in the children. Read a child's result only when it ends.
6. Wake time or nothing left. `100x night end`, disarm the watchdog, then follow the `100x-report` skill. That ranking is the final message. Add every blocked project with its reason, and every project that was never started.

## What the children do

A child is another model, so a child never runs solo. An owner who wants no helpers calls `100x-solo` with a length of work instead, as one brief in one chat.

Each child runs the `100x` pipeline on its own folder, with the wake time as its deadline. At 20 percent of the time left it stops the remaining stages and runs the `100x-wrapup` skill, so every prototype ends working rather than half built. A child for a `--mockup` brief calls `100x-mockup` instead, with its own 15 minute clock, no judge and no wrap up. A retried mockup starts its mockup again, because a mockup never updates `STATE.md`, so there is nothing to resume from. `100x night next` writes all of this into the child's task.

## Safe while nobody watches

`100x ref unattended` has the rules for decisions, credentials, assets and what is never done unattended.

## What is proven

Measured. `100x night` and `100x clock` in tests, including the one at a time hand out, the limit, finished detection from the project's own files, retry and block, and no start in the last hour.
Unproven. A real night of several children in one app. The first one should be watched for the first hour.

# Report

What finished, ranked, what is still being built, and a gallery. Nothing builds.

The owner comes back to several prototypes and decides in minutes which deserve more time. Your job is a ranking they can trust, a plain line on what each run is, the reasons the judge held a run back, where each unfinished run stands, and a page they can click.

Done when the reply has the ranking, what each run is, the reasons for every run the judge held back, every run still in progress, and the page path or URL, and every claim in the reply matches a registry entry.

## Steps

1. Run `100x morning`. It prints the ranking, best verdict first, and writes `~/.100x/morning/index.html`. The command is yours: the owner calls this skill, and you never tell them to run it.
   - The window is `morning.windowHours` (18 by default). "since 2d" after the call is `--since 2d`, and "all" is `--all`.
   - An empty ranking is a result. Say so, then run `100x registry list --all` to look for older runs before concluding nothing finished.
   - A run the page left out because its record is damaged is named in the command's warnings, with the command that drops it. Repeat that warning.
   - Words after the call that are not `all` or a window are a request you do not know. Ask what they want to see, as "When you are not sure" in the `100x` skill says.
2. For clicking, run `100x morning --serve --detach --open`. The page serves from 127.0.0.1 with a random token in the URL. Run starts a prototype's dev server, waits for its port and opens it. Stop ends it. `100x morning --stop` ends the server and every prototype it started.
3. Reply from the ranking, in its words and its order. Draw no table, no second page and no summary of your own over it.
   - One line with the counts. For example "4 finished. 2 ready to ship, 1 fine, 1 needing work."
   - For each run, the ranking's lines: rank, title, what it is, then the moment. A run marked `look` keeps its `look` line and its `why` lines.
   - For the top run, the try-first steps and the run command.
   - Every run no judge looked at, named, with its reason. Every run that needs work, with the single change most likely to fix it. Every failing must-not-break check.
   - After the ranking, the `In progress.` block lists each run that began and has not finished: title, working or idle, its stage, the asks closed, the judge's rounds, and the line that picks it up. Repeat it as written. A run marked idle may have stopped. Say so, and offer `100x-continue` from its folder, or its `100x registry remove` line to drop it from the report. "N older runs never finished" is a count of runs outside the window, and `--all` lists them. A report with no finished run and a run in progress is not empty, so do not say nothing happened.
   - Close with the page path or URL, and the one line that continues the top run: say its folder, and that the owner calls `100x-continue` from there.

## Reading the entries

`look` stands where the verdict would. The builder called the run ready to ship or fine, and something would stop a stranger: a judge who said not ready to ship, no judge, a failed check or a broken screen size. The `look` line says what the builder said and which thing it is. Repeat both, and never turn `look` into a verdict of your own.

Not ready to ship is the usual word after one night, so it is not a failure. The `why` lines say what is behind it. They are the judge's own blockers and majors from its last round, what still stands first. Each ends with what became of it: left for later, fixed but not checked again, or the builder disagreed. Repeat them as written. A `why` line that says the judge left no big finding on record means the judge named nothing big, or its files are gone. Say that, and never make up reasons.

The verdict and its reason come from the run's own core and polish evidence, so repeat them as written. If the reason is thin, say that and recommend the owner look at the hero screenshot and the contact sheet before trusting it.

`REPORT.html` in each project's `.100x` folder is the full trail as a page, including the last decisions and the features with their cut hints. `REPORT.md` has the same in plain text. Open one when the owner asks why. Both start with a `Look first.` line, in red on the page, when something would stop a stranger: a failed check, a broken screen size, no judge, or a judge who said not ready to ship. A judge's no is followed by `Why not ready to ship.` and the same reasons. Repeat both in your reply.

## Housekeeping

- `100x registry remove <id>` drops a run from the gallery. The project folder stays untouched.
- The cards are runs that passed `100x finish`, which refuses to close a run with open asks, a missing review reason or an untriaged finding. A run joins the `In progress` block at its first logged decision and leaves it when it finishes.
- `100x status` inside a project shows one unfinished run in more detail.

# Setup

One question. The owner answers in their own words, as messy as they like. You sort the models into jobs with common sense and save them.

Done when `100x config validate` is clean and the reply shows the jobs as saved, in plain words.

## Voice

Shortest possible. One idea per line, no paragraphs, no preamble. Use the phrases in `100x ref words`. Never show a config key, a setting value or a model id to the owner. Show a model by the name the owner used or the app's list gives, like "Sonnet" or "Opus". Say "judge", not "reviewer". Say "this chat", never "thread". A job with no model of its own shows the model in this chat by name, like "Overnight: Sonnet, same as this chat". Say "max", "extra high" or "high" for effort. Keys and ids appear only in the commands you run.

## Steps

1. `100x config print --sources`. Find the model list for this app, as `100x ref apps` says. In Cursor it is `100x helper models`, after `100x helper setup` and `100x helper login` once. Elsewhere use the app's own list or list command, and `command -v claude codex gemini opencode` shows which other agent apps are installed and can act as the judge. With no list at all, work from what you know and ask the owner to correct the names.
2. Scope. Setup is global unless the owner says "local" or "this project". Local writes `<project>/.100x/config.json` and wins over global, key by key. For a local setup in a folder with no `.100x` yet, run `100x init` first. A global setup needs no project folder, so run no `100x init` for it.
3. Ask one question, exactly in this shape. Nothing before it, nothing after it.

   In Claude Code or the Claude desktop app, or when the owner has mentioned Claude, ask this one. You know your own app, so there is no detection. The answer is a plan, or free text.

   ```
   Which plan are you on? Pick one, or write whatever you want.

   Pro    Sonnet builds, Opus judges. Light: about 3 judge looks a run.
   Max    Opus builds, Fable judges. About 5 looks.
   Ultra  Opus builds, Fable judges. The full run, 8 looks.

   Or in your own words, for example:
   Sonnet max builds. Opus max judges. The small fast one does quick jobs.
   ```

   In Codex, or when the owner has mentioned OpenAI or ChatGPT, ask this one. The plans are in the OpenAI section of `100x ref plans`.

   ```
   Which plan are you on? Pick one, or write whatever you want.

   Go or Plus  Sol builds, Astra judges. Light: about 3 judge looks a run.
   Pro 100     Sol builds, Astra judges. About 5 looks.
   Pro 200+    Sol builds, Astra judges. The full run, 8 looks.

   Or in your own words, for example:
   Sol high builds. Astra high judges. Luna does quick jobs.
   ```

   Everywhere else, ask this one.

   ```
   Which models should do which job? Answer any way you like. Example:

   Sonnet max builds. Opus max judges.
   Codex extra high overnight, and backup judge.
   The small fast one does quick jobs.
   ```

4. Read the answer and sort it. It may name 3 vendors and 7 models at different efforts. Common sense, in this order.
   - **Builds.** The model the owner names for building. Not named: the owner's main or strongest model.
   - **Judge.** The model the owner names for judging. Not named: the strongest model from a different vendor than the builder. Never the builder's own model when another vendor exists. Where `helper.only` is set, the judge is the locked selection and nothing else can start.
   - **Backup judge.** The next model from yet another vendor, or the next strongest. "None" when nothing is left.
   - **Quick jobs.** The fastest or cheapest one the owner names, or the smallest. Not named: the builder's model.
   - **Overnight.** The one the owner names for long runs. Not named: the builder's model.
   - **An OpenAI plan.** The owner says Go, Plus, Pro 100, Pro 200 or Pro 500 instead of, or with, the models. Use the OpenAI section of `100x ref plans` the same way as for Claude, with the same rules. Name each model by family and write the newest version the app lists.
   - **A Claude plan.** The owner says Pro, Max or Ultra instead of, or with, the models. The old names count too: "Max 5x" is Max and "Max 20x" is Ultra. # Solo

One model, one chat, no helpers. The full 100x run, where each second look that a normal run gets from another model is this model attacking its own work, in writing, with proof from running it, again and again.

This is weaker than a second model, and the run says so. A builder cannot see all of its own blind spots. Solo makes it hard on itself in ways a file can show, and `100x finish` refuses what it can check. `100x ref solo` has the rules and the whole procedure. Read it before the first challenge.

Done when `100x finish` has accepted the run, every challenge file passes `100x solo check`, every round and loop file holds its suspicions, and the final message says that no other model looked.

## What changes from `100x`

- **No one else starts.** No subagent, helper, child or judge, for any reason. Where any guide says to start a judge, a backup judge, a fallback or a child, a challenge takes that step instead. Not the Task tool, `100x helper`, `100x review-run`, `100x night`, `claude -p`, `codex exec`, `cursor-agent` or a browser subagent. Tools are fine. Handing work to another model is not. The first three refuse in a solo run, `100x run unset mode` refuses too (the flag is one way), and `100x finish` refuses a run that started one.
- **The same pipeline.** Stages 0 to 8 of the `100x` skill with its stage guides: the prompt, the one thing that must not break, the screens, the report, and the invariants. "No rule, no guess" stays fully on: a `NO RULE` answer from `100x verify cover` still starts the verification procedure, each property is shown to fail before it is trusted, and the ledger is attacked in the `properties` challenge and in every code round.
- **Challenges in place of judges.** Where the pipeline asks a judge, you challenge your own work, in another chair, in a file. `100x ref solo` says where and how.
- **This model judges.** The model in this chat builds and judges, whatever `builder`, `review` and `fallback` say in the settings. Never ask to switch, and never wait for another model.
- **The owner's number phrases** work: `5 rounds of judging`, `for 10 hours`, `3 versions` (one after the other, never at once, each sibling folder its own solo run with `100x run set mode solo` right after its `100x init`, and a dud ending as the variants guide says) and `no verification`. `max N subagents` is dropped, and the first line says so.

## The question

Every challenge starts with it. Ask it of the work as if someone else had made it, and ask it of the running product and the files, never of your memory of making it.

> Let's analyze this. Is it correct? Is it good? Be brutal. Assume it is not, and find out why.

## Steps

1. Stage 0 steps 1 to 4 of the `100x` skill. Solo starts a new run: an unfinished run in this folder that began another way keeps its way, so say that in one line and point to `100x-continue`. After `100x init` run `100x run set mode solo` at once, so a status check, a continue and the CLI know from the first minute. Settle the owner's rules (`100x ref rules`) with this reading: a rule against subagents is what this mode keeps.
2. Step 5, the prompt, and `100x prompt check`. Then the `plan` challenge: `100x solo new plan`, fill it in, and fix `project.md` where it found holes before anything is built.
3. Step 6 and 7. Write `Mode: solo` under Modifiers in `project.md`, and drop `max N subagents`. Step 8, the pre-flight: the line about the model is this one, "Solo: no helpers. I judge my own work and the report says so." Leave out the builder model comparison and the doctor `judge` warning: a solo run is a self-review by design. `100x-setup` stays a "call X" line. The 12 line limit still holds.
4. Stages 1 to 3 as the guides say. At the end of core, build and depth, before the stage's commit and tag: `100x solo new core`, `build` or `depth`, fill it in, fix what broke, `100x solo check`. Core only when a core ran and was not skipped, depth only when features were built.
5. Stage 4. Each pass ends with a loop challenge: write `ask.md`, run `100x review-call --loop pass-N`, which starts nothing and prints the steps, write `judge.md` and then `answers.md`.
6. Stage 5. The red run as the guide says, then `100x solo new properties` when the ledger has rows, and the property attack in `100x ref solo`.
7. Stage 6. The rounds of the `100x-judge` skill, with these changes: `100x brief` and `100x review-call` as usual, and no judge starts. Each round is a round challenge: take the seat the brief names, write the suspicions first, then `findings.md`, then triage, fix and `100x triage`. After the first round `100x run set review '{"status":"reviewed","model":"<this model, as your app names it>"}'`.
8. With a fill clock, arm the watchdog as `100x ref watchdog` says: it is a message into this thread, not another model. Each round of `100x ref fill` ends with a loop challenge, the Skeptic lens and the last stretch are round challenges, and wherever the guide says run the judge you run one. Stage 7 and stage 8 as the guides say, and `100x solo check` before `100x finish`.

A challenge you write after the fact to satisfy the check is worth nothing. Write the suspicions before you run anything, and the findings before you fix anything.

## Reply

The output of `100x finish` is the final message. Add one line of your own: "Solo run: no other model looked at this. The judging was this model checking itself." Point to `100x-report`. End there.

## Rules

- No other model, ever, for any reason. When something needs a second opinion, say so in the final message and leave it to the owner.
- The challenge files are the evidence. A look that left no file did not happen.
- Never write that another model looked, name a judge you did not run, or let a note suggest it.
- Findings before fixes. Triage before changes. Never edit `findings.md` after triage to drop a finding you dislike.
- A short clock shortens the run through the owner's number phrases or through wrap up, never by skipping a look.
- `100x-grind` does not apply: it needs a fresh judge to say yes, and this model cannot be one.
- A solo run fills the window faster than a normal one. Keep `STATE.md` true after every stage and every challenge, and read the files back from disk.

# Wrap up

A deadline and a project that must just work.

Working beats finished. By the deadline one path runs from a clean start, everything unfinished is switched off or removed cleanly, and a short note says what is what. No new features.

Done when a fresh checkout of the branch installs and starts with the written command, the one path ran once with its output kept, `WRAPUP.md` is written, and the work is committed and tagged `100x/wrapup`, with at least 10 percent of the time to spare.

## Steps

1. Model. `100x config target quick`. If it names a model (`{}` means this thread's own model, so there is nothing to compare) and this thread runs another or a lower effort, say so in one plain line and carry on.
2. Deadline. Take it from the message and write it in digits: "by five" is `by 5pm`, "in an hour" is `in 60 minutes`. With none, use 60 minutes, say so and log it with `100x log frame "no deadline given, 60 minutes" "<why>"`. Then `100x init` if the folder has no `.100x`, and `100x clock set "<deadline>"`. Never ask.
3. Branch `100x/wrapup-<yyyymmdd>`, made with `git switch -c`. Stage only files you changed and leave the owner's other uncommitted files untouched.
4. The one path. One sentence in verbs, "A user signs in, adds an item, sees the total". Take it from `.100x/project.md`, the README, the last commits and the routes. Log it with the reason.
5. Inventory by running, not reading. Start the project and try each feature. Mark each as works, half, broken or not started, in `.100x/STATE.md`. Run the project's own tests once and keep the output.
6. Cut plan. Anything not on the path that is half, broken or not started is hidden or removed so nothing leads to a dead end. Prefer hiding behind one flag or one route comment, because it is cheap to bring back. Remove dead buttons, empty pages and half migrations from the visible surface. Write each cut and how to turn it back on.
7. Make the path work. Fix only what blocks it. Stop at the first version that runs end to end. No refactors, no upgrades, no polish unless it hides the path. A fix that would take over a quarter of the time left is replaced by a labelled stub, never an unlabelled fake.
8. Check the clock at every boundary with `100x clock`. At 50 percent used and the path still not working, switch to stubs for the broken part and say so in `WRAPUP.md`.
9. Verify from clean. Commit the work first, staging only your files, because a check of the old commit proves nothing. Then `git worktree add --detach ../wrapup-check`, which checks out that commit and makes no branch. Run the install, the build and the start command there, and run the path once. For a visual project add `100x shots <url> --label wrapup --viewports 390x844@3,1440x900@1` and look. Copy its shots into `.100x/shots/` of the real folder, then `git worktree remove --force ../wrapup-check`. A fix made after this goes back to step 7 and is committed before you verify again.
10. Write `WRAPUP.md`. Works (the path, the run command, the evidence). Cut (each item and how to turn it back on). Known problems (honest, from your runs). Left to do (in order). Time (finished at, minutes spare).
11. Commit `WRAPUP.md` and the shots, tag `100x/wrapup`. Stop every dev server. `100x log done "wrapup" "<what works>" "<the path output>" done`.

## Reply

Eight lines at most. Works or not first. The run command. What was cut. Known problems. No questions.

## Rules

- No new features, no dependency upgrades, no schema or data changes.
- No deploy. A preview only when the project already has one configured and the owner asked for it. Never production.
- No sound. Mute every browser you drive.
- If the path cannot work before the deadline, say that at the halfway mark in `WRAPUP.md` and wrap up what does work.
